impTopics.title: Linked List Data Structure: Concepts, Advantages, and Applications
impTopics.description: A linked list is a linear data structure consisting of nodes connected in a sequence, where each node contains its own data and a reference to the next node. Linked lists are dynamic, allowing memory allocation as needed, and are commonly used for implementing insertion, deletion, stacks, and queues. However, they have drawbacks such as wasted memory due to pointer storage, sequential access for element retrieval, and difficulty in reverse traversing. Linked lists find applications in creating trees, graphs, and other data structures.

impTopics.title: Circular Linked List Operations: Insertion, Deletion, Traversal
impTopics.description: Circular linked lists can be either singly or doubly linked, with no beginning or ending. In a circular singly linked list, traversal occurs until the starting node is reached, with no null value in the next part of any node. Operations on circular lists include insertion at the beginning or end, deletion at the beginning or end, searching, and traversing. An example code snippet for insertion at the beginning involves creating a new node, updating pointers, and adjusting the head node accordingly.
